sens: What remains of a whole after a part has disappeared or been removed
A surviving group after judgment or destruction
The faithful people preserved by God amid judgment
G9577.detail:
1. The remnant refers to what remains, what physically subsists: for example, when a part is taken from a whole, a portion remains. This is the simplest image of the word.
2. In a context of judgment or catastrophe, the remnant is what survives, what escapes destruction: the survivors of a disaster, those who are not swept away.
3. Specifically, the remnant of Israel is the people that God faithfully preserves, despite judgment. In Romans 9:27, Paul quotes Isaiah: even if Israel were as numerous as the sand of the sea, only a remnant will be saved. This is a divine certainty: God never leaves His people completely annihilated; He always keeps a faithful portion.
G9577.origine: The word comes from ancient Greek and literally means "what is left under" (ὑπό, "under," and λείμμα, "what is left"). In the Greek Old Testament, it regularly translates the Hebrew שָׁאַר (shaar), which also means "to remain, to subsist." This notion of remnant is very important in biblical theology: God never completely rejects His people; He always preserves a faithful remnant.
G9577.emploi: The word appears only once in the New Testament, in Romans 9:27, where Paul uses it to quote the prophet Isaiah. In this pivotal passage, Paul addresses the apparent rejection of Israel: why have so many Jews not believed in Jesus? He answers by invoking the "remnant": there has always been, even in the worst moments of judgment, a faithful remnant that God preserves. This thought of the remnant runs throughout the Old Testament (Elijah, the survivors of Babylon, etc.), and Paul applies it to the time of the Gospel: only a remnant of Israel recognizes Jesus as Messiah, but this remnant is the true continuation of the people of God.
G9577.portee: This notion of remnant is deeply comforting for the Christian. It reminds us that God never gives up on His people, even when evil seems to triumph or faith appears to be in the minority. It also teaches that salvation is not a matter of numbers or carnal power, but of divine faithfulness. For Israel as well as for the Church, God keeps a people for Himself, even in times of crisis or general unfaithfulness.
